title: Spelling Word Lists
keyIdea: The Year 3 and 4 word list in England has about 100 words that children often misspell, such as February, separate, believe, address and knowledge. Most of each word follows the usual patterns; usually one part is hard. Four tricks help with that part: say it in a spelling voice to hear letters you skip when you talk (Feb-ru-ar-y), find a hidden word (there is a rat in separate), check for double letters (address has two d), and find the root word (knowledge comes from know). Then check those words in your own writing.
familyTip: Pick one list word a day, such as surprise or library. Ask your child to say it in a spelling voice, beat by beat, then write it without looking. Then make up a silly memory hook together for the hard part, like 'never believe a lie'.

visual.caption: Which trick helps with each word? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: say words in a spelling voice, find hidden words, choose one letter or two, find the root word and check a sentence.

kid: Some words are hard to spell, even when you know them well. Your school has a list of them for Years 3 and 4. February, separate and believe are on it.
Most of a hard word is easy. Only one part is hard. A trick for that part helps you remember it.

Trick 1: say it in a spelling voice. We say Feb-yoo-ary, but it is spelt Feb-ru-ar-y. Say each beat slowly, and you hear the r. Trick 2: find a hidden word. There is a rat in separate. Never believe a lie.

Trick 3: look for double letters. You hear one d in address, but it has two. Trick 4: find the root word. Knowledge comes from know, so it starts with a k you do not hear. After you write, check the list words. Read them slowly, the way they are spelt.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. English Appendix 1 of the national curriculum in England gives a statutory word list for Years 3 and 4. It has about 100 words that are often misspelt, such as accident, believe, different, February, knowledge, library and separate. Pupils should spell them, and the standards expect them to be used correctly in writing.

Most of each word is regular, so the job is to find the part that breaks the rule and learn that. Four strategies cover most of the list. A spelling voice (saying Feb-ru-ar-y or busi-ness as written) brings back letters that speech skips. A hidden word gives a hook (a rat in separate, a lie in believe, an ear in heart). Some words need a check for double letters (address, appear, opposite, occasion). For others, the root word gives the start (favour in favourite, appear in disappear).

Common mistakes: writing what you say, such as Febuary, libary, suprise and probly; swapping vowels, as in seperate and beleive; doubling the wrong letter or not doubling at all, such as adress, dissapear and imagine with two m; and spelling a word right in a test but wrong in a story. Careful: a hook only helps if it fits the hard part. A pear in appear does not tell you about the double p.

In the lab your child drags the letter we skip into six words, finds the hidden word in five more and chooses one letter or two in six. Then they pick the root word for five words and find the misspelt list word in five sentences.

practice.prompt: Which spelling of the second month is right?
practice.hint: Say it slowly in a spelling voice: Feb-ru-ar-y.
practice.explain: February has two r: Feb-ru-ar-y. We often skip the first r when we talk.

practice.prompt: Ella learns {n} list words a week. How many has she learned after {w} weeks?
practice.hint: Each week adds the same number of words.

practice.prompt: Which small word hides inside separate and helps you spell it?
practice.hint: The hard part is the middle of the word.
practice.explain: sep-a-rat-e: there is a rat in separate, so the middle letter is a, not e.

practice.prompt: A list has {t} words. Sam can spell {k} of them. How many does he still need to learn?
practice.hint: Take the words he knows away from the whole list.

practice.prompt: Which word has a double letter?
practice.hint: Say each word in a spelling voice.
practice.explain: address has two d: ad-dress. imagine has one m and calendar has one l.

pool.prompt: Which spelling of believe is right?
pool.hint: Look for the hidden word lie.
pool.explain: Never believe a lie: b-e-l-i-e-v-e has lie in the middle.

pool.hint: Say it in a spelling voice: sur-prise.
pool.explain: surprise starts with sur. We often skip that r when we talk.

pool.prompt: Which root word helps you spell knowledge?
pool.hint: Which word has the same meaning at its heart?
pool.explain: knowledge comes from know, so it starts with a silent k.

pool.prompt: A spelling test has {q} list words. Mia gets {r} wrong. How many does she spell right?
pool.hint: Take the wrong ones away from all the words.

pool.prompt: How many letters s are in business?
pool.hint: Say it in a spelling voice: bus-i-ness.
pool.explain: bus-i-ness has one s in bus and two at the end: three in all.

pool.prompt: Things vanish. Which spelling is right?
pool.hint: Build it from dis plus the word appear.
pool.explain: dis + appear: one s from dis and two p from appear.

pool.prompt: Which word in this sentence is spelt wrong? 'We went to the libary on Friday.'
pool.hint: Say each word slowly, the way it is spelt.
pool.explain: It is library: li-brar-y has two r.

pool.prompt: What is the best way to learn a hard list word?
choices: find the hard part and use a trick for it
pool.hint: Most of the word is easy. One part is not.
pool.explain: Find the part that breaks the rule and use a trick, like a spelling voice or a hidden word.

pool.prompt: Which word has just one m?
pool.hint: Not every middle letter is doubled.
pool.explain: imagine has one m: i-ma-gine, and it ends in e.

pool.prompt: Ben's story uses {s} list words. When he checks them, he finds {w} spelt wrong and fixes them. How many were right the first time?
pool.hint: Take the ones he had to fix away from all the list words.
pool.explain: {s} − {w} = {=s-w} list words were right before he checked.
